title: Leadership Profile: Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory – A Man of Connections and Humility
content:
Leadership Profile: Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory – A Man of Connections and Humility
1. Introduction: The Uncrowned Leader of the Generation of Connections
The leadership of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of blessed memory was radical precisely because it was built on foundations—humility, unconditional love and deep listening—that are often perceived as the antithesis of modern conceptions of power and influence. He held no official title that defined his standing, yet he acted as a "great connector" in Israeli society, a personality whose entire being was a mission of mending rifts and building bridges. This profile will analyze his unique philosophy of leadership, which turned these spiritual principles into an ordered and powerful method, and its profound influence on social and religious movements in Israel.
His extraordinary ability to bridge the political and social divides that define contemporary Israel was not a by-product of his personality, but a direct result of his teaching. Evidence of this can be found in the words of the state's leaders, who recognized in him a figure belonging to all of Israel. The President of the State at the time, Reuven Rivlin, described him as one who was "a lover of peace and a pursuer of peace, loving people and bringing them near to the Torah," while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defined him as a "great connector" who worked for "unity and love of Israel." These perceptions did not grow in a vacuum; they were a precise expression of an entire philosophy of life.
To understand the secret of his influence, one must go beyond the outward descriptions of his work and delve into the fundamental philosophical principles that formed the basis of all his actions. His leadership was not a collection of actions, but a practical expression of an ordered worldview, whose foundations we will now examine.
2. The Core of His Thought: "A School of Humility"
Understanding Rabbi Wishlitzky's leadership requires delving into the philosophical foundations that guided him. Humility, unconditional love and seeing the good were for him not merely personal character traits, but an ordered and comprehensive method that formed the basis of all his public, educational and personal actions. He was, as people testified of him, a walking "school of humility," in which every spiritual principle was translated into daily practice. An analysis of these fundamental principles reveals the inner engine that drove one of the greatest enterprises of connection Israeli society has known.
2.1. Humility (Anavah) as the Foundation of Everything
At the center of Rabbi Wishlitzky's teaching stood the trait of humility, which he saw as "the root of faith" and the basic condition for any repair of the world. An analysis of his figure reveals a powerful paradox: humility, in his conception, was not an expression of weakness or outward modesty, but a conscious strategy of emptying oneself of the private "I." It was this self-emptying that created the inner space which allowed him to be a clean channel for a message greater than himself, and to connect authentically and without ego with others and with the mission. Thus, precisely the nullification of the "I" became a source of immense inner strength and wide-ranging influence.
His deep humility was expressed in every detail of his life:
He consistently refused to sit in places of honor, and even avoided sitting in the chair of a rosh yeshiva younger than himself, saying: "Who am I that I should sit at all?"
He used the word "I" so rarely that his students noted that it was hard to find it in his words.
In his original interpretation, he explained that the biblical expression "Let us make man," said in the plural, is a lesson in humility from the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself, teaching that "the greater one consults and takes permission from the lesser."
His figure, described as "a school of humility," taught that only out of self-emptying can sincere, deep and long-term influence grow.
2.2. Unity and Unconditional Love (Ahavat Yisrael)
The principle of "Ahavat Yisrael" (love of the Jewish people) was the central driving force of Rabbi Wishlitzky's activity. It was not a sentimental feeling, but an ordered theological principle that served as the engine of his public activity. It was based on the ruling of the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself, as the Ben Ish Chai interpreted it, that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir: "Either way they are called children." That is, the status of Israel as the children of the Holy One, blessed be He, is never annulled. The mechanism that enabled him to love unconditionally without giving up criticism rested on a sharp distinction: love is always directed toward "the pure soul," the eternal divine part of a person, while education and rebuke relate solely to outward actions.
This principle was expressed consistently and impressively in his work:
In interpreting the commandments: Rabbi Wishlitzky interpreted everyday commandments as mental exercise for strengthening brotherhood. The commandment of returning lost property, for example, he saw as training to "remember the brotherhood and forget the hatred"—to strengthen the living memory of the inner bond that unites and to make people forget the outward factors that divide.
In public action: After the painful split in the "Mercaz HaRav" yeshiva and the founding of the "Har HaMor" yeshiva, Rabbi Wishlitzky was the only figure who continued to teach in both institutions at once. This was not merely a gesture of reconciliation, but a practical expression of his principled commitment to unity, which saw every Torah scholar as part of the divine whole, above every dispute.
In unconditional love: He stressed that one must love even those who do not observe the Torah and the commandments, while distinguishing between love of the person (the soul) and criticism of his actions. Love, he explained, is directed toward the inner force, while the negation relates to outward behavior alone.
2.3. The "Good Eye" as a Methodology
The concept of the "good eye" was a central working tool in Rabbi Wishlitzky's leadership. It was not naive optimism, but systematic "work" and a conscious effort to identify the point of life and goodness in every person and every situation. In his method, "advocacy" (sanegoria) is not a surrender of the truth, but "deep and broad wisdom" that makes it possible to uncover the inner and deeper truth, even when it is covered by outer layers.
He interpreted the concept of "guarding the eyes" in a revolutionary way: not as passive avoidance of seeing evil, but as an active and constant search for the good in every Jew. This, he said, was what the Baba Sali meant when he said that the secret of his power lay in "guarding the eyes"—the ability "to see good in every Jew."
His initiative to set up WhatsApp groups called "The Merits of Israel," in which positive stories about the people of Israel are passed on every Saturday night, illustrates his method in practice. In this way he sought to amplify the positive, to flood the world with the good, and to make dealing with the merits of Israel a way of life and a methodology for repairing the world.
3. Leadership in Action: From the Field of Thought to the Field of Deeds
These philosophical pillars were not abstract ideals confined to the walls of the study hall; for Rabbi Wishlitzky they formed an explicit master plan for action. The following chapter analyzes how he systematically translated his "Torah of connections" from the field of thought into a nationwide social enterprise. His leadership was a leadership of constant movement, of going down to the field and of physical presence wherever he felt he was needed, out of a sense of deep and uncompromising commitment to the whole of Israel.
3.1. A Life of Mission: The "Samuel the Prophet" of the Generation
Rabbi Wishlitzky's life was conducted as a life of constant "mission." He saw himself as a soldier in a great campaign, whose task was to move ceaselessly in order to connect, strengthen and illuminate. The image that stuck to him, "the Samuel the Prophet of the generation," aptly expresses his unceasing journeys throughout the country, like the prophet who made the circuit of the cities of Israel. The sense of mission was so deeply ingrained in his essence that it defined his identity absolutely.
3.2. The Enterprise of the Torah Core Groups: Leadership of Integration
As "the rabbi of the Torah core groups" (garinim toraniyim), the spiritual companion and compass of one of the most significant social enterprises of Religious Zionism, Rabbi Wishlitzky instilled a model of leadership that flowed directly from the principle of humility. He opposed the conception of the core groups as a "conquering" or "rescuing" force coming to redeem the periphery, and demanded that they act from a place of integration.
His central guideline was to join the veteran communities humbly, to learn from them, to receive from them, and to exert influence out of an inner, true and sincere connection. He rejected the pride of "we are the elite unit," and in its place coined the guideline "and go to the vessels"—to be a receptacle, to receive from the place and serve it, and not to come from a position of condescension. This model made the core groups a connecting and growth-giving force, and not an alienating one.
3.3. Redrawing the Map: "The Natural Towns"
One of the most powerful expressions of Rabbi Wishlitzky's leadership was the conceptual revolution he coined in changing the term "development towns" to "natural towns." This was not a merely semantic change, but a fundamental reversal of the social value system in Israel. It was a revolutionary act of leadership, which redefined center and margins not by economic or geographical criteria, but by spiritual and moral standards.
Behind this change stood an entire ideology: the belief that in the periphery, in cities such as Dimona, Sderot and Beit She'an, are found "the natural people"—sincere and genuine people who are not enslaved to "the externality of life" and to the superficial culture of the West. In his eyes, it is precisely Tel Aviv and the cities of the center that are the true "development towns"; places whose residents need "to develop their souls" and free themselves from enslavement to an external culture, to money and to honor. In this way he not only gave honor and pride to the residents of the periphery, but also set a deep spiritual challenge before Israeli society as a whole.
4. The Wishlitzky Method: Personal and Pedagogical Style
Rabbi Wishlitzky's personality and style were inseparable from his messages. How he taught and led was no less important than what. His power stemmed from the complete correspondence between what he said and who he was, between his teaching and his being. He did not only speak of humility, love and listening—he lived them. This chapter will focus on the methods of action and the unique style that characterized him and made every meeting with him a formative experience. We will examine three key aspects of his method: the art of listening, the ability to translate spiritual ideas into practice, and the power of the personal bond.
4.1. "Before He Would Say Anything, He Would Listen"
The methodology of deep listening was a precondition for Rabbi Wishlitzky's influence. He did not come to "pour out" his teaching, but sought first of all to understand the person or community before him. As Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu testified of him: "Before he would say anything, he would listen... listen to people, listen to the stirrings of their hearts... and only after he had listened... then he would say something."
His words resonated powerfully not because they were a universal truth, but because they were precisely attuned to "the stirrings of the heart" of the person before him, and made that person feel seen and understood even before he had learned anything. This approach made his words relevant and precise. They did not stem from a predetermined agenda, but grew out of an authentic connection to the need, the pain or the question of the other side. Therefore they were received "like living water to a weary soul."
4.2. From Spirit to Matter: Translating Principles into Life
One of Rabbi Wishlitzky's great strengths was his ability to "translate" abstract spiritual ideas into practical guidelines and into a relationship with everyday events. He connected the upper worlds with the most earthly reality, and showed how every act, however small, is an arena for the service of God.
Pride and driving: He knew how to link the abstract trait of pride with everyday actions such as using a remote control to open the car or dangerous driving on the road, and showed how the sense of "I" is expressed there too.
The Traveler's Prayer and using a cellphone: In a pointed and unforgettable statement, he determined that for one who touches a cellphone while driving, his "Traveler's Prayer" is "a blessing in vain." In this way he turned caution on the roads into a deep spiritual matter.
Disengagement and engagement: He did not define the struggle against the Disengagement Plan as a merely political struggle, but as a spiritual struggle against the conception of "disengagement" as a whole. The remedy, in his view, was "engagement"—connection between the parts of the people, between a person and himself, and between the people and its land.
4.3. "Everyone Felt That He Was His Best Friend"
Above all, Rabbi Wishlitzky is remembered for his wondrous ability to create a personal, deep and warm bond with every person he met. Countless testimonies describe a similar experience: the feeling that at that moment his whole being was given over to the person before him, as if that person were the center of his world.
His personal bond was not abstract, but tangible and physical. Many testimonies described again and again the warm and genuine embrace, the strong handshake that "transmitted strength and energy," and his physical presence at difficult moments—sometimes "without words," just to be there and support. He "set his eyes and his heart" on each person, as the Midrash required of Moses our teacher. It was this rare ability that enabled him to be so great a connector; connection was not ideology alone, but a personal and tangible experience that everyone who met him had the privilege of experiencing.
5. Legacy and Influence
The legacy of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky extends far beyond his life. It lies not only in his books, but first and foremost in the thousands of people and the social enterprises he brought into being, which continue his path. He left behind him not buildings or titles, but living souls and a paved way of life, whose influence is measured not in official achievements but in the deep change he brought about in people's hearts.
The main points of his legacy lie in several foundational elements:
The "middle bar" of the generation: More than anything, Rabbi Wishlitzky served as a uniting force—the "middle bar" of the Tabernacle, which connects all the parts into one complete structure. He was the glue that mended rifts in the public, who worked tirelessly to connect extremes, to bridge gaps, and to remind everyone of the deep common denominator.
Imparting the "Torah of connections": Rabbi Wishlitzky not only lived connection, but left behind an ordered method—"the Torah of connections." This teaching, based on humility, the good eye, love of Israel and mission, continues to serve as a beacon for his students and for everyone who seeks to work for unity and goodness among the people of Israel.
Leadership of responsibility: His central legacy is an eternal call to personal and national responsibility. He taught by his deeds that every person must leave the private space and personal comfort, "take your tiredness with you... and travel," and be an active partner in the process of the redemption of the people of Israel. This is a call not to be passive, but to initiate, to connect, and to be part of the great story.
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory: A Biography of a Man of Connection and Humility
Introduction: A Man of Mission and Love of Israel
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of blessed memory was an exemplary figure of connection and love in Religious Zionism. He devoted his whole life to one great task: love of the Torah, of the people of Israel and of the Land of Israel. He was not the rabbi of a single institution, but a rabbi of many, "a rabbi of connections" who worked in every corner of the country out of an infinite sense of mission. Alongside his greatness in Torah, he was known for his deep humility and his self-sacrifice, qualities that made him a figure loved and admired by thousands. Since his death on 25 Tevet 5779, his absence has been deeply felt in the hearts of many who continue to walk in his light.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Roots and the Shaping of His Path: His Early Years
To understand Rabbi Wishlitzky's life's work, one must go back to his early years, where his special personality was formed and his spiritual path was set.
Childhood and family background: Rabbi Elisha was born in 5714 (1954) in Kvutzat Yavne. His parents, Shlomo-Salomon, a native of Oświęcim, and Bilha-Berta, a native of Berlin, were people who had survived the inferno of the Holocaust and chose to build their home in the Land of Israel.
The world of the yeshiva: After his studies at Midreshiyat Noam, Rabbi Elisha came to the "Mercaz HaRav" yeshiva in Jerusalem. There he became a distinguished disciple of the great figures of the generation in Religious Zionism, who stamped their spiritual and ideological imprint on him. His principal teachers were:
Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook of blessed memory
Rabbi Yehoshua Zuckerman of blessed memory
Rabbi Zvi Israel Tau, may he live long
His bond with the yeshiva and its way was deep and essential, as Rabbi Yehoshua Zuckerman, one of his foremost teachers, testified of him in a eulogy:
"Rabbi Elisha represented Mercaz HaRav at its best, perhaps in the most beautiful way."
These years in the yeshiva were formative years. They deepened his love of the Torah, shaped his redemptive worldview, and prepared him for his life's mission—to spread the great light he had absorbed from his teachers throughout the country.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Life's Work: Leadership of Connection in the Field
Rabbi Elisha was not a man of official titles, but a man of the field who worked tirelessly wherever he was called. His leadership did not stem from an appointment, but from broad public recognition of his greatness and devotion. This wide-ranging activity did not stem from mere activism, but grew out of an ordered and profound spiritual teaching—a "Torah of connections"—that illuminated every step of his way.
Father of the Torah core groups: Rabbi Wishlitzky was one of the founders of the enterprise of the Torah core groups and was known by the nickname "the rabbi of the core groups." He saw them as a central tool for connecting the parts of the people and strengthening Jewish identity. For decades he traveled ceaselessly throughout the country, "from Eilat to Kiryat Shmona," in order to strengthen, accompany, advise and be with the members of the communities.
His conception was revolutionary and founded on deep humility. He guided the members of the core groups not to come as "saviors" or condescendingly, but to join the veteran communities respectfully. His message was sharp and clear: "You have not come to save the town; you have come humbly to join the veteran residents... receiving from them and bringing what you too can contribute." With this approach he coined terms that turned the accepted conception on its head:
"The natural cities": a name for the cities of the periphery, in which, in his view, live sincere and genuine people who are not enslaved to Western culture.
"The development towns": a name for the cities of the center, whose residents, he said, need to develop their souls and free themselves from externality.
A man of connections, not of titles: Although he held no official position as "rosh yeshiva" or "city rabbi," Rabbi Wishlitzky was a central and active figure in dozens of institutions and organizations. Every place became a home to him, and every person became a friend.
Deep social involvement: Rabbi Wishlitzky was a man who lived the pain of the community and shared the burden with his fellows at all times. His devotion was expressed especially during the period of the Disengagement Plan, when he devoted himself heart and soul to the residents of Gush Katif. He became part of them, sat with them whole nights on the sidewalks in Neve Dekalim, listened, embraced and strengthened the spirits of young people and adults alike. During periods of rocket attacks on Sderot, he traveled to the south to be with the residents and show a shared fate. And when he heard on the radio about a crisis at the "Pri Galil" factory in the north, he immediately changed his plans and traveled specially to the place to be with the workers, sing with them and lift their spirits. None of these were symbolic acts, but a living expression of deep love and a true connection to the pain of Israel.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Spiritual Teaching: "The Torah of Connections"
Rabbi Wishlitzky's teaching was not merely theoretical; it was a Torah of life, based on several fundamental principles that recurred in his lessons and his deeds.
A school of humility: For Rabbi Elisha, humility was not merely a character trait, but "a complete method" and "the foundation of his strength." He fled from honor as from fire, disliked using the word "I," and never agreed to sit in the first row or at the head table. When he introduced himself, he would say simply: "Elisha from Jerusalem." This humility was not a pretense, but a deep worldview that a person is an emissary, and it was this that opened hearts to him and enabled him to create genuine connections with every person.
Love and the "good eye": seeing the good in every Jew. Rabbi Wishlitzky taught a revolutionary conception of the concept of "guarding the eyes." He related how Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu of blessed memory once asked the Baba Sali of blessed memory what the secret of the power of his blessings was. The Baba Sali replied: "Guarding the eyes." And when asked what this meant, he explained: "To see good in every Jew." Rabbi Wishlitzky made this principle one of the pillars of his teaching: guarding the eyes is not only avoiding forbidden sights, but an active and constant search for the good point in every person. He believed in **"love without conditions"**, and taught that just as we ask the Holy One, blessed be He, to love us unconditionally, even in a generation "that curses its father and does not bless its mother," so we are obligated to love our children and the whole of Israel—a love that does not depend on anything.
Truth and peace: Inspired by the verse from Zechariah, "Love truth and peace," Rabbi Wishlitzky held together the two values, which sometimes appear contradictory. He did not give up the truth and could be demanding and incisive, but he always did so out of tremendous love and a desire to connect. His ability to speak harsh words of rebuke that were accepted by his listeners stemmed from the fact that his words were wrapped in such great love and humility that they opened the heart instead of closing it.
Refinement of character and mission: The rabbi stressed that a "religious" person is measured first and foremost by the commandments between a person and his fellow. He saw his whole life as a divine mission, and this awareness gave him superhuman strength. As Rabbi Dov Bigon testified, "When a person is an emissary, the mission gives him strength." This conception was the engine behind his tireless activity. Even during his severe illness, when he was exhausted and in pain, he continued his journeys throughout the country and said that the travels and the meetings with the people of Israel were "his medicine."
Rabbi Wishlitzky's unique teaching, which combined greatness in Torah with simple humility and infinite love of people, left a deep mark on his tens of thousands of students, who continue to walk in his light.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Legacy: The Middle Bar of the Generation
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky was "the rabbi of connection of the generation." He himself used the image of "the middle bar" of the Tabernacle—that hidden board which connects all the parts of the Tabernacle into one unit without standing out itself. So he acted all his life, and so he instructed his students to find their place: "Who said you were born to be a board? Perhaps you were born to be the last millimeter in the 'middle bar'... Take your tiredness with you, put it in some side bag on your shoulder, and travel."
The immense affection he enjoyed was expressed at his funeral, attended by thousands from every part of Israeli society, and in the many testimonies of people each of whom felt that the rabbi had been "his best friend." As an expression of deep appreciation for his work, a street was named after him in the city of Sderot, the city he so loved and strengthened.
Rabbi Elisha's legacy lies not only in his books and lessons, but in the resounding call to continue the "melody" of connection, humility and love of Israel that was his whole life.
The Foundations of the Teaching of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory: A Guide for Beginners
Introduction: The Man of Connections and Humility
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of blessed memory was a prominent figure in Religious Zionism, known for his deep love for the people of Israel, the Torah of Israel and the Land of Israel. All his life he acted as a "great connector," who bridged gaps and disputes in Israeli society. All this out of a worldview whose roots are planted in humility and infinite self-sacrifice, which sets a challenging spiritual path before us.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 1: Humility – The Foundation of Everything
At the center of Rabbi Wishlitzky's teaching stands the conception that humility is the absolute foundation of a proper spiritual life and of the service of God.
1.1. "A School of Humility"
For Rabbi Wishlitzky, humility was not merely a positive character trait, but a complete worldview, which he called "a school of humility." He taught that true humility is a necessary condition for attaining the fear of Heaven and a pure love of the Land of Israel. This insight is summed up in his saying:
"One who hopes to merit the removal of pride from his heart will merit the love of the Land of Israel."
1.2. Divine Humility as a Model
Rabbi Wishlitzky interpreted the expression "Let us make man" from the Book of Genesis as a lesson in humility from the mouth of the Almighty. He explained that the Holy One, blessed be He, so to speak, "consulted" with the ministering angels before creating man. In this way the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself taught that the trait of humility is the strongest shield against pride, which is the root of heresy.
1.3. Humility in Practice
Rabbi Wishlitzky lived the teaching of humility with his whole being. Two examples illustrate this:
He used to introduce himself simply as "Elisha from Jerusalem," and avoided using titles.
When he was offered a seat at the head of the table or in a place of honor, he firmly refused, saying: "Who am I that I should sit at all?"
Only out of emptying the self and recognizing the magnitude of our task, as humility demands, can there grow the inner space needed for the great mission of his life: unconditional love for the whole of Israel.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 2: A Mission of Connection and Unconditional Love
Rabbi Wishlitzky's central mission was to connect people, to bridge gaps and to instill the principle of love that does not depend on anything (love without conditions).
2.1. Remember the Brotherhood, Forget the Hatred
Rabbi Wishlitzky saw the commandments between a person and his fellow as tools for building national unity. He laid special stress on the commandment of returning lost property. In his view, the main purpose of the commandment is not only the technical act of returning an object, but a deep training of the soul "to remember the brotherhood and forget the hatred," and to see the inner bond of the soul that unites all the parts of the people of Israel.
2.2. "Either Way They Are Called Children"
His teaching on love without conditions was based on the teaching of Rabbi Meir, and can be summed up in the following points:
Unconditional love: Just as a parent's love for a child does not depend on anything, so the love of the Holy One, blessed be He, for the people of Israel is absolute.
"You are children of the Lord your God": The rabbi stressed that even when the people of Israel sin, their status as the children of the Holy One, blessed be He, does not change. He taught, following the Ben Ish Chai, that "God, blessed be He, ruled the halakha according to Rabbi Meir."
Refraining from accusation: The natural result is that one must never accuse any part of the people of Israel or disqualify it, even if it is a generation that seems completely lost.
Love that does not depend on anything cannot remain an abstract idea; it must be embodied in deeds. Therefore Rabbi Wishlitzky saw in the meticulous observance of the commandments between a person and his fellow the most concrete and precise expression of love of Israel.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 3: The True Test: Religiosity Between a Person and His Fellow
Rabbi Wishlitzky did not ask whether a person is religious, but how his religiosity is expressed in the world. In his view, the true test is not in the synagogue but in the marketplace, on the road and at home.
3.1. Beyond Ritual
Rabbi Wishlitzky's central argument was that the title "religious" must apply to a person who is meticulous in all parts of the Torah, and especially in the social and moral commandments. In his "school of humility," grades were not given for the strictness of ritual, but for meticulousness in the social commandments.
3.2. A Torah That Touches Life
The following table illustrates how Rabbi Wishlitzky interpreted the commandments between a person and his fellow as lessons in building character and building society:
This commitment to every person in Israel broke the accepted boundaries of "religiosity," and obliged him to break the geographical boundaries of "center" and "periphery" as well and to set out on a journey of connections throughout the country.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 4: A New Map of Israel: "The Natural Towns" and a Mission to the Whole
Rabbi Wishlitzky had a unique conception of the geography of Israel, which led him to a life of tireless mission.
4.1. Reversing the Map: Center and Periphery
Rabbi Wishlitzky proposed a reversed view of the concepts of "center" and "periphery" in Israel.
"The natural towns": the cities of the north and the south, which in his opinion were populated by more "natural" and authentic people, who are not enslaved to the superficiality of Western culture.
"The development towns": the cities of the center of the country (Gush Dan), whose residents, in his conception, are the ones who need to "develop" their inner spiritual world and free themselves from materialism.
4.2. A Life of Mission
Rabbi Wishlitzky's life was a life of constant mission. He traveled ceaselessly from one end of the country to the other, from Eilat to Kiryat Shmona, sometimes visiting several remote communities in a single day. He did this not only in order to teach, but in order to be with the people. He saw in this bond the purpose of his life and the source of his strength, even when he was ill and exhausted.
4.3. "The People of the Border"
Rabbi Wishlitzky developed the concept of "the people of the border" from the words of the Mishnah in Tractate Sotah, and gave it three topical interpretations:
The geographical border: the pioneers and residents of the periphery, whose idealism and devotion are pushed to the margins by the center.
The border between the holy and the profane: people who know how to bridge between different worlds and to contain complexity. He noted that in a period of polarization such people are not popular.
The moral border: leaders who set a moral bar and challenge the public to improve from within, instead of saying only things that are pleasant to hear.
This unceasing journey to "the people of the border" in all their senses would have worn out any person. But Rabbi Wishlitzky drew his strength from one spiritual principle, which was both a condition of the mission and its result: the ability to see with a good eye the infinite good hidden in every person and every place.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary: A Legacy of the Good Eye
Rabbi Wishlitzky's legacy is not merely a collection of ideas, but a call for an inner revolution: to begin with humility, to act out of love, and to see the good hidden in the people of Israel as the task of our lives. The fundamental principle driving this whole teaching is the power of the "good eye." He taught, in the name of the Baba Sali, that the true meaning of "guarding the eyes" is not an act of avoidance, but the positive and active choice "to see good in every Jew." It is a constant call to adopt a gaze that discovers the inner good hidden in the people, to serve it with boundless devotion, and to know that the strength comes from the task itself. As he taught:
"According to the tasks, so are the strengths."

title: Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory
content:
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory
This text surveys the life, profound thought and public legacy of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky, a key figure in modern Religious Zionism. The source details the foundations of his teaching, which stress the centrality of the refinement of character, the rejection of sectoral partitions and a deep spiritual connection to the residents of the periphery, which he called "the natural towns." Beyond the conceptual aspect, the text describes his practical work as **"the father of the Torah core groups"** and as a founder of the "El Ami" movement, while presenting the institutions and projects established to commemorate his educational path. This survey reflects his unique attempt to translate the teaching of redemption into pioneering social action that seeks to uncover the inner Jewish point in all parts of the nation.
The Torah Teaching, Educational Work and Public Influence of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky of Blessed Memory
Biography and Formative Stations in His Life
Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky was born on 1 April 1954 (27 Adar II 5714) in Kvutzat Yavne.[1] He was born to Shlomo-Salomon, a Holocaust survivor born in the town of Oświęcim in Poland, and to Bilha-Berta, a native of Berlin.[1] The family background of his parents, who had experienced the destruction of European Jewry and rebuilt their home in the Land of Israel, was a significant layer in the shaping of his national identity and his deep commitment to the building of the nation. In his childhood his family moved to the Kiryat Shmuel neighborhood of Haifa, where he absorbed the local values of Torah and labor.[1]
He did his high-school studies at Midreshiyat Noam, after which he turned to higher studies at the Mercaz HaRav yeshiva in Jerusalem.[1, 2] In this yeshiva he became one of the distinguished disciples of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook and Rabbi Yehoshua Zuckerman.[1, 2] From these teachers he received his redemptive Religious Zionist teaching, his commitment to the whole of Israel and the readiness to act in the field of national education and outreach out of a pioneering and uncompromising approach.
Rabbi Wishlitzky married Chaya and set up his home in the Givat Shaul neighborhood of Jerusalem.[1] His family combined in practice the world of Torah with significant security service; his son, Yehuda Wishlitzky, was awarded a Chief of Staff's citation for his conduct and fighting in the grave armored personnel carrier incident in the battle of Shuja'iyya during Operation "Protective Edge" in 2014.[1] His daughter, Hodaya, married Rabbi Lior Lavi.[1]
In 5779 the rabbi suffered a heart attack and was hospitalized in critical condition in the intensive care unit.[1] He died on 25 Tevet 5779 (2 January 2019) at the age of 64.[1] His mass funeral, attended by thousands of his students and admirers, set out from the Machon Meir yeshiva, passed by the Mercaz HaRav yeshiva, and he was buried in the Prophets' section of the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives.[1]
Public recognition of his work grew after his death through wide-ranging municipal and educational commemoration projects. Streets were named after him in Sderot (in 2020), in Kiryat Malakhi (in 2023) and in Jerusalem (in 2023).[1] In 2025 a square was dedicated in his name in the Kedmat Zion neighborhood of Jerusalem, and at the same time Torah and educational institutions bearing his name and his educational vision were established in Rosh HaAyin and in Akko.[1]

Foundations of His Torah Teaching and Public Thought
The Torah thought of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky draws on the school of Rav Kook (the Ra'ayah) and his son Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook (the Ratziyah), but it is characterized by a practical, social and psychological translation of the ideas of redemption and faith into the reality of modern life.[1, 2] His thought can be characterized by means of several central paths that express an original and incisive view of Israeli society.
The Centrality of the Refinement of Character and of the Commandments Between a Person and His Fellow
Rabbi Wishlitzky saw the refinement of character and moral behavior as the inner and necessary gate to any religious and spiritual progress.[1] In his view, the observance of the commandments cannot be reduced to technical or ritual aspects alone, such as meticulous adherence to the laws of kashrut or outward embellishments.[1] He stressed that the true service of God is measured first and foremost by uprightness of heart, a good eye, humility and the quality of relations between a person and his fellow.[1] Without this moral infrastructure, the whole religious edifice remains empty of inner content and misses its divine purpose.
Rejection of Sectoral Labeling and Social Partitions
The rabbi firmly opposed the accepted sectoral division of Israeli society.[1] He adopted and developed the teaching of Rav Kook (the Ra'ayah), according to which separating and divisive titles such as "religious," "Haredi" or "secular" must disappear entirely from Jewish parlance.[1] He held that these definitions are external and artificial, and that their effect is to arouse division between the parts of the nation instead of uncovering the shared soul and the point of Jewish selfhood present in every person.[1]
The Geography of the Spirit: "The Natural Towns" versus "the Development Towns of Gush Dan"
One of Rabbi Wishlitzky's most original conceptions concerned the geographical and cultural division of the State of Israel.[1] The rabbi showed warmth and immense appreciation for the cities of the periphery in the north and the south, which he made a point of calling "the natural towns."[1] In his view, the residents of the periphery preserved mental health, existential simplicity, innocent faith and a direct connection to the tradition of the fathers, because they had not been enslaved to alienated externality and to Western consumer culture.[1]
By contrast, the rabbi euphemistically called the established and affluent cities of Gush Dan "development towns."[1] With this name he sought to express the view that it is precisely the residents of the center who need the "development" of their soul and spirit, and that they must undergo a process of liberation from the foreign influences of the culture of Europe and the United States, which place materialism, outward achievement and social alienation at the center.[1]
His View of Current Affairs and His Attitude to the Media
Rabbi Wishlitzky sharply criticized the main media outlets in Israel, which he defined as "an imaginary power with nothing behind it."[1] He saw the media as a factor that produces false impressions, magnifies disputes and systematically weakens the national spirit. This independent position found stormy expression when he was among dozens of rabbis who signed a letter of support for former President of the State Moshe Katsav after his conviction.[1] In a lesson he gave that same week he explained his motives, while attacking the conduct of the media and what he saw as a ruthless public trial by mob.[1]
His redemptive conception stressed inner contemplation of the processes of the generation.[3] He gave regular lessons on "the teaching of redemption," "the essence of the war against Amalek" and the meaning of Jerusalem as a city "joined together," with an emphasis on the fact that the modern process of redemption involves deep self-clarification and the strengthening of the national powers of the soul.[3]

The Enterprise of the Torah Core Groups and the "El Ami" Movement
Rabbi Wishlitzky's public work was characterized by constantly going out of the study hall into the public field, out of the understanding that a Torah that does not meet the broad public lacks its national dimension.
Father of the Torah Core Groups and Keren Kehilot
Rabbi Wishlitzky is considered one of the central and most influential founders of the enterprise of the Torah core groups in Israel, and was even given by his admirers the title "father of the core groups."[4] He saw the Torah core groups as a strategic tool for the social and spiritual renewal of the cities and neighborhoods of the periphery, not out of a paternalistic approach of one-directional "bringing hearts closer," but out of deep partnership and mutual learning with the local residents.[4] The rabbi worked tirelessly within the "Keren Kehilot" organization—the umbrella organization that unites and empowers the Torah core groups throughout Israel.[1] His contribution was expressed in personal accompaniment of the members of the core groups, in charting a spiritual path and in frequent travels to the far corners of the country to strengthen the families working in the field.[1, 4]
The El Ami Movement and Its Northern Branch "El Ami – El Atzmi"
Rabbi Wishlitzky was one of the founders of the "El Ami" movement, established by disciples of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook with the aim of engaging in education for faith and spreading Judaism among the broad public.[1, 5] The movement, whose headquarters are located in Ma'alot-Tarshiha, held many seminars and produced a variety of study and outreach materials.[5] As early as around 1980 the movement initiated the establishment of a pioneering Torah core group in the city of Eilat, which served as a prototype for the entire enterprise of the core groups.[5]
Over the years the movement's northern branch developed and became an independent association called "El Ami – El Atzmi," which employs some 150 people, among them permanent staff, lecturers, instructors and volunteers.[5] The association operates a long series of educational and social projects with broad nationwide reach, while integrating young women in national service within the framework of "Zehut – the Association of Centers for Jewish Identity."[5]

Educational and Torah Institutions Established in His Spirit
Rabbi Wishlitzky's educational and Torah legacy finds tangible expression in the establishment and operation of educational and Torah institutions throughout the country that adopt his educational teaching, which places trust in the person and love of the Land at the center of activity.
These institutions put into practice the pedagogy of Rabbi Wishlitzky, who sought to raise God-fearing students of good character, engaged with the world of action and technology out of a sense of mission and national responsibility.[6]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Literary Enterprise and the Digital-Communal Commemoration Project
Rabbi Wishlitzky left behind a rich literary harvest dealing with the clarification of the powers of the soul, the struggle of faith in the period of "the birth pangs of the Messiah," and the refinement of character on the private and national levels. His books divide into those published in his lifetime and books edited and reconstructed from his many lessons after his death.
The "Parasha ve-Nefesh be-Chevlei Mashiach" Project and the Subscription Model
As part of the effort to make the rabbi's Torah teaching accessible to the broad public, a unique project called "Parasha ve-Nefesh be-Chevlei Mashiach" (Torah Portion and Soul in the Birth Pangs of the Messiah) was established.[14] The project operates in the format of ongoing crowdfunding through a "subscription donors" model.[14] Within this framework, donors commit to a fixed sum (ranging from 10 ₪ for a small booklet to 40 ₪ for a full book), which is collected only when a new book or booklet is published (once every one to three months).[14] In return, the donors receive a digital edition of the book in their email inbox.[14]
These donations serve directly to finance the project's various stages: producing weekly booklets on the Torah portions of the week (which are to be gathered into books), producing special booklets and books for the festivals of the year, and producing short materials suited to rapid digital distribution.[14] In more advanced stages the project aims to establish a nationwide system of lessons and study groups based on the foundations of the rabbi's teaching.[14]
Spreading Torah by Digital Means
In the years since the rabbi's death, the "Bishvil ha-Neshama" association has been working to spread his teaching in dozens of WhatsApp groups and in Sabbath leaflets throughout the country.[14] This distribution includes short weekly materials from his lessons, and every Saturday night moving stories that judge the people of Israel favorably, from the week just past, are sent out in the WhatsApp groups, as a direct continuation of the way of the rabbi, who championed seeing the good and the good eye.[14]

Summary and Intellectual Assessment
An analysis of the work and Torah teaching of Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky reveals a unique personality that combined absolute loyalty to the study-hall tradition of the Mercaz HaRav yeshiva with a groundbreaking sociological and social view of Israeli society.[1, 2] His greatest public contribution was turning the Religious Zionist theory of the redemption of Israel into a living, breathing enterprise of action in the field through the Torah core groups and the "El Ami" movement.[1, 4, 5]
Rabbi Wishlitzky was not content with theoretical study of the concepts of the community and the nation; he demanded that his students go out to "the natural towns," connect with the simplicity and faith of the broad public, and act out of humility and a good eye.[1] His rejection of sectoral labeling and his uncompromising demand to place the commandments between a person and his fellow at the top of the spiritual ladder constitute a vital call for direction for Israeli society.
The many commemoration projects established in his memory—from yeshiva high schools and hesder programs in provincial towns, through a digital distribution network for his lessons, to communal publishing projects—testify that his teaching and educational path continue to serve as a moral and spiritual beacon for thousands of students and followers, who work ceaselessly for the building of society and spirit in the State of Israel.[1, 6, 14]
